Theophilus of Antioch
thee-OF-il-us
proper noun
Greek Theophilos, “lover of God” or “loved of God,” a bishop of Antioch in the second century.

Biblical Definition

Theophilus was bishop of Antioch in the latter half of the second century, and the author of three books addressed To Autolycus, a heathen friend who mocked the faith. In them he defended the one living God, the creation of the world out of nothing in the beginning when God created the heaven and the earth (Gen 1:1), the inspiration of the Scriptures, and the resurrection. He is remembered above all as the first writer known to use the word Triad of the Godhead, naming God, His Word, and His Wisdom, and so giving the church an early term for the doctrine that the Lord taught when He bade the apostles baptize in the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Ghost (Mat 28:19). The dictionary honours Theophilus as a defender of the truth of Scripture and an early witness to the Trinity. He met the scoffer not with the wisdom of the Greeks but with the testimony of the prophets, holding that all Scripture is given by inspiration of God, and is profitable for doctrine (2Ti 3:16). His witness to the eternal Word, who was with God and was God (Joh 1:1), stands among the seeds from which the great Trinitarian confessions of the church afterward grew.

Webster 1828 Definition

A second-century bishop of Antioch, defender of Scripture and the first known writer to use “Triad” of God.

THEOPHILUS OF ANTIOCH, a bishop of Antioch in the second century.

He wrote three books To Autolycus, defending the faith to a heathen friend.

He set forth the one God, creation, the inspired Scriptures, and the resurrection.

He is the first writer known to use the word Triad of the Godhead.

His witness stands among the early seeds of the Trinitarian confession.

Key Scripture

Gen 1:1 — "In the beginning God created the heaven and the earth."

Mat 28:19 — "Go ye therefore, and teach all nations, baptizing them in the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Ghost:"

2Ti 3:16 — "All scripture is given by inspiration of God, and is profitable for doctrine, for reproof, for correction, for instruction in righteousness:"

Joh 1:1 — "In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God."

Modern Corruption

He answered the scoffer not with Greek wisdom but with the testimony of inspired Scripture and the early confession of the Triad.

expand to see more

The corruption Theophilus answered was the cultured contempt of the heathen for the Scriptures, the scoffing of an Autolycus who would not believe what he had not seen. The dictionary honours the bishop’s reply, which rested not upon the wisdom of the Greeks but upon the witness of the prophets and the inspired word of God.

Theophilus is honoured chiefly for his early naming of the Triad, an instance of how the church, taught by Scripture, came to speak with growing precision of the one God in three Persons. The doctrine was not invented by the fathers but confessed by them, drawn from the baptismal charge of Christ and the opening of John’s Gospel. The dictionary receives such early witnesses gladly, while holding, as they did, that the rule of all doctrine is the inspired Scripture and not the speculation of men.

Hebrew Roots

From the Greek for “lover of God,” Theophilus names a second-century bishop of Antioch.

Theophilus — Greek Theophilos, “lover of God.”

He was bishop of Antioch in the second century.

He wrote three books To Autolycus in defence of the faith.

He defended creation, inspired Scripture, and the resurrection.

He first used the word Triad of the Godhead.

Usage

"Like Theophilus, answer the scoffer with the inspired Scripture, not the wisdom of the Greeks."

"The Triad he named is the one God in three Persons, confessed and not invented by the church."

"All Scripture is given by inspiration of God, and is profitable for doctrine."
